newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Canadian Pacific merger shows trend.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canadian Pacific merger shows trend.

text.p: The consolidation sweeping through the container shipping industry took another stride on Wednesday with the unexpected news that Canadian Pacific Ltd had agreed to acquire Contship Containerlines Ltd.

The merger, which is likely to be completed by the end of September, will give Canadian Pacific's subsidiary CP Ships annual revenues of more than C$2 billion from carrying more than one million twenty foot equivalent container units (teu) each year.
CP Ships' latest acquisition comes just a fortnight after it completed the controversial purchase of bankrupt U.S. container line, Lykes Lines Ltd for $30 million.

But the CP Ships' deals are only the latest in a string of mergers and acquisitions within the container shipping industry that have been driven by overcapacity and intense competition which has provided thin profit margins. Shipping industry analysts believe there can only be more to come.

Last autumn, UK shipping and property group P&O group announced the merger of its container shipping operations with Nedlloyd Lines, part of Koninklijke Nedlloyd Groep NV. Earlier this year Singapore's Neptune Orient Lines Ltd said it planned to buy Oakland-based APL Ltd for $825 million.

While those two deals have made headlines in the business press world-wide, there have been a number of acquisitions and mergers among smaller players, indicating the trend affects not only the largest firms.
Private French shipowner Compagnie Maritime d'Affretement won the mandate to buy state-owned Compagnie Generale Maritime, and South Korea's Hanjin Shipping Co Ltd bought Germany's DSR-Senator Lines.

A year earlier, South Africa's Safmarine won majority control of Belgian container shipping firm CMB Transport. Ironically, Safmarine admitted on Wednesday it had also made a bid for Contship Containerlines, but it lost out to CP Ships.
Driving the shipping lines eagerness to merge are the twin aims of cutting costs and reducing competition.

Despite container shipping volumes rising a healthy rates each year for more than two decades, the increases have at each stage been more than offset by increasing in shipping capacity as established lines attempted to enlarge their trade share and new lines sought to gain a foothold.
Many believe the current rash of mergers has been triggered by the fears of the huge volume of new ships about to be delivered from the world's shipyards.
Of the world's fleet of large containerships over 3,000 teu, the equivalent of an other 42 percent are currently on order, according to shipbroker Clarksons.

These competitive pressures have lead container freight rates to fall to record lows on many of the world's major liner routes, especially those between the Europe and Southeast Asia/Far East and across the Pacific.

But while rates have been on the slide, demands for investment in new equipment - from larger faster ships to new technology - have seen capital costs in the container shipping industry spiral, further eroding profitability.

Mergers help cut costs, the lines argue. P&O Nedlloyd said it intended to take out over $200 million in costs per year. It is now thought that figure may reach $250 million. Neptune Orient said it also expected savings from its merger with APL, albeit at a lower level.
In addition, the lines privately admit that mergers also eliminate competition, helping them regain some control over the trades they once dominated through the cartels known as shipping conferences.
Trends towards consolidation in the container shipping industry also reflects the increased corporatisation within the shipping industry as a whole.
More shipping companies are choosing to gain stock market listings, or are merging with competitors to gain economies of scale.
As with all the most obvious trends, there are always exceptions, of course.
Recently, New Jersey-based Atlantic Container Line AB said it had abandoned its hope to find merger partner for its North Atlantic container and vehicle shipping operation.

And some major container companies, such as the Maersk Line of Denmark's A.P. Moeller Group and CSX Corp container shipping subsidiary Sea-Land Service, have vowed to maintain close operating partnerships, rather than undertake outright merger.
Yet the industry's direction for the foreseeable future appears set.

"There is one thing for certain, there will be more mergers in the container shipping industry," commented a London shipping analyst, who declined to be named. "The only question is which companies, and when."
